title: Exposed Customer Data: Choosing Protections
context: A sales team exports a customer file for a campaign. The file contains names, emails, card numbers, and dates of birth. Three decisions are required.

n1.text: Card numbers must be stored in the payment database. Which method limits risk without breaking the process?

choices.text: Display them in plaintext in the application to simplify support
choices.why: Plaintext exposure increases theft surface and PCI DSS compliance scope.

choices.text: Replace them with tokens and display only the last 4 digits
choices.why: Tokenization at storage and masking on display: the two protections are complementary.

choices.text: Hash them with SHA-256 in the database
choices.why: A hash is not reversible: it does not allow retrieving the card for a payment.

n2.text: The export file must be shared with a partner for statistical analysis. What is the best approach?

choices.text: Send the full file via encrypted email
choices.why: Encryption protects transit, but sends unnecessary personal data to the partner.

choices.text: De-identify the dataset, then restrict access by role
choices.why: De-identification reduces personal data scope and least privilege limits access.
Partial: other fields (name, date of birth) allow re-identification.

n3.text: Which role should bear final responsibility for this data?

choices.why: The owner decides classification and access rules; the custodian implements the controls.

choices.text: The developer who wrote the export script
choices.why: The developer implements, they do not define data policy.
The processor is a third party handling data, not the data owner.

n4.outcome: You distinguished tokenization, masking, de-identification, and data protection roles.

debrief: Tokenization = controlled reversible substitute; masking = hiding on display.
De-identification reduces the scope of shared personal data.
Data owner = decision and classification; data custodian = implementation of controls.
